Crohn's disease (Crohns sygdom) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease and one of the two main forms of [[inflammatoriske-tarmsygdomme|Inflammatoriske tarmsygdomme]] (IBD), alongside [[colitis-ulcerosa|Colitis ulcerosa]] [^src6]. It is a central focus of clinical monitoring within the [[dansk-kvalitetsdatabase-for-inflammatoriske-tarmsygdomme|Dansk Kvalitetsdatabase for Inflammatoriske Tarmsygdomme]] (DANIBD) [^src7]. In the Danish healthcare system, patients are included in the DANIBD registry if they have at least two hospital contacts with specific action diagnoses in the [[landspatientregisteret|Landspatientregisteret]], including the code DK50* for Crohn's disease [^src7].

Epidemiologically, Crohn's disease is the most frequent diagnosis among both newly diagnosed and prevalent children and adolescents with [[ibd|IBD]] in Denmark [^src1] [^src4]. During the reporting period from October 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, 57% of newly diagnosed children had Crohn's disease, with a majority being boys (61%) and most diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 17 (50%) [^src1]. In the subsequent reporting period from October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024, out of 751 children and adolescents with IBD in contact with hospital departments, 27% were newly diagnosed, and among these new pediatric cases, 64% had Crohn's disease [^src4]. In this later cohort, boys accounted for 53% of the new cases, and 89% were diagnosed between the ages of 10 and 17 [^src4]. Among the prevalent pediatric population, Crohn's disease also remained the most common diagnosis, accounting for 55% of cases in the earlier period [^src1].

Clinically, the disease often requires surgical intervention, making post-operative follow-up a critical quality indicator for patient care [^src2] [^src3] [^src5]. The systematic tracking of Crohn's disease and other IBD subtypes allows DANIBD to evaluate treatment quality, monitor biological and targeted synthetic drugs, and ensure standardized care across Danish regions [^src2] [^src4] [^src5].
